title: Retrieval lab: name the missing evidence before repairing the run
goal: Retrieve the cycle's controls from symptoms, locate the first unproven boundary, and repair only after the failed state is understood.
tag: Certification retrieval and gap session · cycle 4, position 7
concept:
A parcel tracker can say “label created” even though the carrier never received the box. One green checkpoint does not prove the whole trip.

A data release has four separate claims: the trigger woke the graph, transformation produced the right candidate, publication changed the live version, and serving capacity met demand. Retrieval practice means naming which claim lacks evidence before choosing a repair. A gap is recorded as “not yet demonstrated,” never guessed from silence.
example: A payments file arrives at 8:52. The graph starts, but the transform fails. The dashboard still reads version 43 from yesterday. The correct first statement is not “the trigger is broken” or “add a cluster.” It is “transform success is unproven.” After the cause is fixed, rerun the failed work and its dependent publication, then check the live version and query queue.

use_case.when: Use a retrieval/gap session after several related lessons or before a certification practice set, especially when many controls can produce similar symptoms.
use_case.example: A morning data product is stale even though an arrival trigger fired; the team must distinguish trigger, transform, quality, publication, and serving evidence.
use_case.decision: Start at the first unproven boundary and request its native evidence. Repair from there. Do not infer personal mastery from lesson delivery; only an explicit answer or real sandbox result can close a learner gap.

practice: Choose the observed incident. Predict the first missing proof, then compare it with the evidence ladder before selecting a repair.
boundary: This local diagnostic uses four fixed stages and synthetic states. It does not query either vendor, reproduce permissions, concurrent runs, retries, task-history retention, data correctness, cloud-event delivery, or real query latency.

'+x+'

'+m[1]+': '+m[2]+'.

';};gapCase.onchange=paintGap;paintGap();

Whether transformation completed
Whether more serving clusters are needed
Whether the live table should be dropped
Trigger evidence only proves wake-up; transformation is the next boundary.
Why repair from the first failed task and its dependents?

Retrieve before revealing. A triggered task graph ended FAILED. The graph summary names the first error task; TASK_HISTORY supplies task-level error details and query IDs. Only then consider retry.

title: allOf waits for every future—even after one has already failed
goal: Use CompletableFuture.allOf as a completion barrier without mistaking it for fail-fast cancellation or a result collector.
concept:
Three couriers carry parts of one report. If one courier reports a failure at noon, the coordinator still waits for the other two to report back before declaring the group complete.

CompletableFuture.allOf returns a new future that completes when every supplied future completes. If any child completed exceptionally, the aggregate completes exceptionally. The aggregate does not contain the child values; inspect them individually. It also does not promise to stop the other computations.
example: Inventory succeeds, payment fails, and shipping is still running. The payment failure does not make allOf done yet. When shipping completes, the aggregate becomes done and exceptional. Inventory and shipping results still exist in their own futures.

use_case.when: Use allOf when independent asynchronous work must all reach a terminal state before a final step, report, or cleanup decision.
use_case.example: A backend loads inventory, payment risk, and shipping quotes in parallel before assembling an order view.
use_case.decision: Use it as a barrier, not a cancellation policy. Add explicit fail-fast signaling and cooperative cancellation when continued sibling work is wasteful or unsafe. Inspect child futures when individual results or errors matter.

practice: Move the failure and slow completion across three futures. Predict when the aggregate becomes done and which child values remain available.
boundary: The Java replay uses manually completed futures for deterministic ordering. It proves allOf completion semantics, not executor scheduling, interruption, network cancellation, exception selection among multiple failures, timeouts, structured concurrency, or resource cleanup.

No; it waits for shipping to complete too

The returned future completes only after all supplied futures complete.

allOf is a Void barrier; child results remain on the children.
When is allOf alone insufficient?

title: Page for action now; ticket work that can wait
goal: Separate urgent actionable symptoms from useful but non-pageable operational evidence.
tag: Distinguished Engineer · monitoring and on-call design
concept:
A smoke alarm wakes you because you must act now. A note that its battery will expire next month belongs on a maintenance list.

A page interrupts a human. It should represent a user-visible symptom or an imminent hard failure, and the on-call must have an action. A cause metric such as high CPU can help diagnosis without being the page itself. If something matters but can wait, track it as planned work instead of teaching people to ignore alerts.
example: Checkout errors exceed the SLO and traffic can be shifted: page. CPU is 85% but users are healthy: record and investigate, not a page. A storage quota is 99% and crossing it will instantly stop writes: page because immediate preventive action exists.

use_case.when: Use this decision when an organization has noisy alerts, missed incidents, or on-call fatigue despite extensive monitoring.
use_case.example: A Spark platform pages on every executor-memory spike while missing a sustained data-freshness breach that customers actually experience.
use_case.decision: Page on urgent symptoms with a tested action. Allow cause-based preventive pages only for an imminent cliff with action now. Put non-urgent defects into a tracked queue; keep diagnostic metrics on dashboards.

practice: Classify four signals by urgency, user impact, and actionability. Watch the route change when one of those conditions is missing.
boundary: The model uses fixed classifications. Real paging needs SLOs, burn windows, deduplication, severity, ownership, dependencies, maintenance handling, notification delivery, human factors, and periodic review of false positives and misses.

Question: Should this interrupt the on-call?

Actionability: '+m[2]+'. Route: '+m[3]+'.

';};pageSignal.onchange=paintPage;paintPage();

title: Return a resource link when the model does not need the whole file yet
goal: Keep large MCP resources out of the immediate tool result while preserving a client-controlled fetch path.
tag: GenAI harness engineering · MCP resource links
concept:
A library catalog gives you a title and shelf location. It does not photocopy a 400-page book into every search result.

An MCP tool may return a resource_link with a URI, name, description, and media type instead of embedding the resource bytes. The client can fetch or subscribe when needed. Tool-returned links are not guaranteed to appear in resources/list, so the harness must preserve the returned link itself.
example: A search tool finds a 20 MB Parquet profile. Returning a link keeps the immediate result small and lets the host decide whether to read it. Embedding may still fit a tiny configuration file that the model needs now. A link is not authorization: the client still needs safe URI handling and access checks.

use_case.when: Use a resource link when a tool discovers a large, binary, optional, or lazily consumed artifact.
use_case.example: A data-quality tool returns a profile report, Spark event log, or lineage export that only a follow-up diagnostic needs.
use_case.decision: Embed small essential text that the next model step truly needs. Link large or optional resources. Preserve provenance, enforce URI and authorization policy, and do not assume a link is present in resources/list.

practice: Change file size and delivery mode. Observe whether bytes enter the immediate result or remain behind a client-controlled fetch boundary.
boundary: The model counts synthetic bytes and assumes one link record. It does not implement an MCP transport, resources/read, subscriptions, authentication, URI allowlists, redirects, MIME validation, content scanning, caching, range reads, or model context limits.

title: One fibre can be both the display wire and the touch map
goal: Understand how a one-dimensional digital fibre can support an interactive two-dimensional garment interface.
concept:
A normal screen is a flat sheet of pixels. Cloth is woven from long threads. The hard part is not merely making a glowing thread; it is addressing many pixels and locating a touch through the same textile-friendly structure.

The reported digital pixel fibre combines addressable pixels, a shared interconnection along the fibre, and a coaxial sensing layer that localizes touch. The authors integrated fibres into a sleeve with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30 frames per second, and 8-bit colour depth.
example: Think of eight teaching fibres with eight pixel positions each. A touch at fibre 3, position 5 maps to one cell, and the shared bus updates that cell. The paper's garment is much larger—5,184 display pixels—and also integrates multimodal input/output. This is a research prototype, not evidence that any shirt can become a production computer.

use_case.when: Use this research when evaluating future human–machine interfaces that must remain flexible, washable, breathable, and textile-like.
use_case.example: A specialist garment could combine touch controls with physiological, inertial, optical, or acoustic sensing without attaching one rigid phone-sized panel.
use_case.decision: Treat the paper as evidence for integrated interactive textile architecture. Product selection still needs independent evidence for manufacturing yield, power, comfort, repairability, wireless security, long-term washing, heat, cost, accessibility, and target-task usability.

practice: Move a touch across a teaching weave. Watch one fibre and one along-fibre position intersect to select a pixel, then compare the toy grid with the reported 96 × 54 prototype.
boundary: The grid is an original address-mapping model. It does not reproduce the paper's materials, coaxial sensing, resistive paths, circuits, colour, refresh behavior, wash tests, wireless system, multimodal sensors, power, computation, or measured durability.

title: An OIDC token states who asked; the AWS trust policy decides who enters
goal: Bind GitHub Actions cloud access to exact audience and subject claims, including the current immutable subject format.
tag: CI/CD security · GitHub Actions OIDC to AWS
concept:
A building badge states a person's identity. The door's access list decides whether that identity may enter.

GitHub's OIDC token carries claims such as aud and sub. AWS evaluates those claims in the role trust policy. For repositories created after July 15, 2026, or older repositories that opt in, the default subject includes immutable owner and repository IDs. A trust policy written for the old name-only format will not match that token.
example: The production role requires audience sts.amazonaws.com and subject repo:acme@12/payments@34:ref:refs/heads/main. The main job matches. A feature branch and another repository receive valid GitHub tokens but AWS denies them because their subjects differ.

use_case.when: Use GitHub OIDC when workflows need short-lived AWS credentials without storing long-lived cloud secrets.
use_case.example: Only the payments repository's protected main deployment may assume an EKS production-deployer role.
use_case.decision: Match audience and a narrow subject in AWS. Confirm whether the repository uses mutable or immutable subject format before rollout, update cloud trust before changing GitHub's template, and add environment protection when the subject references an environment.

practice: Switch the token source and trust-policy format. Observe that token issuance is not AWS authorization and that a stale name-only policy denies an immutable token.
boundary: The model compares two strings. It does not mint or validate JWTs, verify issuer/signature/time, model custom claims, GitHub Enterprise Server, environment protection, IAM permissions policies, role sessions, forks, reusable workflows, Dependabot, AWS STS, or compromise scenarios.

title: A saga compensation is a new business action—not a database rewind
goal: Use compensating transactions to restore business intent across service-owned databases while making failed compensation visible.
concept:
A hotel cannot erase yesterday. If a trip is cancelled, it creates a cancellation and refund; it does not rewind every system to an earlier instant.

A saga splits one business transaction into local service transactions. If a later step fails, compensating transactions perform business reversals. Compensation can also fail, so the workflow needs durable state, idempotent commands, retries, and a visible manual-repair path.
example: Order creates order O-42, Inventory reserves one item, then Payment declines. The orchestrator sends ReleaseInventory and CancelOrder. If release succeeds, the business outcome is cancelled with inventory available. If release fails, the system is not “rolled back”; it is in a repair-required state.

use_case.when: Use a saga when one business operation spans service-owned databases and holding a distributed lock or global ACID transaction is unavailable or undesirable.
use_case.example: An order spans Order, Inventory, and Payment services with independent persistence and potentially long-running steps.
use_case.decision: Prefer one local transaction when the data belongs in one service. Use a saga only with explicit compensations, durable orchestration/choreography, idempotency, concurrency rules, observability, and product-approved meanings for partial or irreversible effects.

practice: Fail payment, then fail or succeed inventory release. Follow each service's durable state and identify the exact outcome the customer can be told.
boundary: The model is a single-order orchestrated saga. It omits message delivery, outbox, duplicate commands, timeouts, concurrent orders, isolation anomalies, refunds, irreversible email/shipping effects, authorization, compensation ordering, workflow durability, and data reconciliation.

questions: Payment declines after inventory is reserved. What should happen?
Issue a ReleaseInventory compensation and cancel the order
Delete every service database
Pretend the reserve never happened
Compensation is a new local business transaction that reverses the reservation's intent.
Inventory release also fails. Is the saga rolled back?
No; it needs durable retry or manual repair
Yes; all databases return automatically
Yes; the payment decline deletes the reservation
Compensations can fail, leaving an explicit incomplete business state.

All affected data belongs in one service and one local transaction works
Services own separate databases
The business process is long-running

walkthrough.limit: The model is a single-order orchestrated saga. It omits message delivery, outbox, duplicate commands, timeouts, concurrent orders, isolation anomalies, refunds, irreversible email/shipping effects, authorization, compensation ordering, workflow durability, and data reconciliation.

visual_explanation: The three service records remain visible through forward failure and compensation, so the learner sees a new cancelled state rather than a fictional time rewind.
